To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) spider fearful girls showed greater approach avoidance tendencies than spider fearful boys, and (ii) the AAT was a valid test for automatic behavioral avoidance tendencies.

(1) children show an automatic avoidance tendency towards spiders, but not towards butterflies or neutral stimuli, and (2) girls who report more fear and show more anxious behavior towards spiders in other tests also show a greater avoidance tendency towards spiders in the AAT.
(1) the AAT is a useful tool to assess automatic avoidance tendencies in children and (2) girls with higher fear of spiders and higher anxiety behavior show a greater avoidance tendency on the AAT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the approach-avoidance task as a measure of behavioral avoidance tendencies in spider-fearful children and the relationship between the AAT and self-reports and behavioral measures.
the evaluation of a new task for the study of avoidance tendencies in children, and with the study of sex differences in this tendency.
the development and validation of the AAT for the measurement of approach and avoidance tendencies in spider fearful children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the AAT is a valid and useful measure of automatic behavioral tendencies in children.
the AAT is a valid and reliable measure for the assessment of approach and avoidance tendencies in spider fearful children.
girls who report more fear of spiders and show more anxious behavior in the BAT also show greater avoidance tendencies in the AAT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the AAT may be a useful test of automatic avoidance tendencies in children and may be a useful addition to the assessment of spider fear in children.
children who report greater fear of spiders show greater avoidance tendencies in the AAT and greater anxiety in response to spider stimuli in the BAT.
the AAT can be used as an experimental tool to assess automatic behavioral tendencies to approach and avoid stimuli related to a fear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the AAT may be a useful tool to assess automatic avoidance tendencies in children, and may be a useful adjunct to the BAT.
the AAT can be used in children as young as 9 years old, and that this test can be used to assess avoidance tendencies in spider fearful children.
the AAT is a promising tool for the assessment of behavioral avoidance tendencies in spider fearful children.
